analysis.one_liner: Puts cigarettes and other tobacco products under FDA regulation, with minimum-age sales rules and stronger warnings.
analysis.headline: A bill to regulate tobacco under the FDA, backed by 54 House members, never received a committee vote and died at the end of the 103rd Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, no federal agency had authority over how cigarettes were made, sold, labeled, or advertised. This bill would have put tobacco under the same Food and Drug Administration rules that cover other products people ingest: a ban on sales to anyone under 18, disclosure of additives and smoke constituents, larger 'Smoking is Addictive' warning labels, a ban on brand sponsorships of public events, manufacturer registration and inspection, and annual fees on manufacturers to fund FDA oversight. It would have stopped short of banning tobacco outright.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people: the roughly 3,000 children who the bill's findings say try cigarettes each day, smokers who would get fuller information about additives and addiction, and nonsmokers exposed to secondhand smoke. The bill's own findings state tobacco causes about 450,000 deaths and $65 billion in lost productivity and health care costs each year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, smokers, and nonsmokers exposed to smoke

how_it_helps.text: Bars sale or distribution of tobacco products to anyone under 18, establishing a federal minimum age of sale where none existed [S3]

Requires labels to disclose chemical additives and smoke constituents like benzene, arsenic, and cyanide, and replaces one carbon-monoxide warning with 'Smoking is Addictive. Once You Start You May Not Be Able to Stop' [S3]
Makes it unlawful for tobacco brands to sponsor public sporting or cultural events, and subjects tobacco advertising to rules consistent with those for prescription nicotine products [S3]
Requires manufacturer registration, factory inspection, and annual fees based on market share to fund FDA enforcement, and bans free samples and coupon distribution [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would face registration, inspection, disclosure of ingredients, advertising and sponsorship restrictions, and annual fees scaled to market share. Those costs and fees would likely be passed on to consumers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Annual manufacturer fees and compliance costs would raise production costs that companies could pass on to consumers in higher prices [S3]

The bill does not ban tobacco sales, so it would not reduce the product's core health harms, only its marketing and sale to minors; the Secretary is expressly barred from outlawing tobacco solely because it causes disease [S3]

A good-faith objection: placing tobacco under drug-style regulation expands federal authority over a legal product and over advertising, which industry and some members argued belonged with the FTC and state law [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is large by the bill's own findings, about 450,000 deaths a year, and the main costs fall on tobacco companies and their marketing, with modest price pass-through to consumers. The bill is deliberately narrow, protecting existing sales rather than banning the product, so its real-world impact would depend on how FDA wrote the rules. On balance the costs fall mainly on the industry being regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment subcommittee until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995, and no markup, vote, or floor action ever happened.

narrative.text: The bill's findings state that tobacco causes roughly 450,000 deaths and $65 billion in annual costs, and that no federal agency had authority to regulate tobacco's manufacture, sale, labeling, or advertising [S3]
It was introduced on May 18, 1993 by Rep. Mike Synar with 9 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5]
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on June 25, 1993, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S5]
It drew 53 additional cosponsors, 47 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but never advanced out of committee [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers are better off: federal regulation of their product, which this bill would have started, never happened during this Congress, so manufacturing, marketing, and sales continued under the same rules as before.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had broad bipartisan sponsorship, 47 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but it never reached a vote, so no recorded opposition pattern exists in this Congress.

industries.note: The bill would impose registration, FDA factory inspection, ingredient disclosure, advertising limits, sponsorship bans, and annual market-share fees on cigarette and smokeless tobacco makers, whose product the bill's findings link to 450,000 deaths a year. Its interest ran against the public-health rules the bill would create.

industries.industry: Advertising and event sponsorship (sports and cultural events)
industries.note: The bill would make it unlawful for tobacco brands to sponsor public events under their names, ending a major promotional channel worth a share of the roughly $4 billion the industry spends yearly on promotion per the bill's findings.
